title: The order coroutines start in
prompt: `launch` does not run its body immediately.
explanation: `launch` creates a coroutine and by default (`CoroutineStart.DEFAULT`) queues it on the dispatcher rather than running it at once. The current coroutine carries on to its first suspension point — printing `2` — and only at the `delay` does control pass to the launched one. With `start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED` the order would be `1 3 2 4`.

title: async and parallelism
prompt: Two requests of 100 ms each — how long do they take together?
explanation: The two `async` calls start at the same time, and `await` waits for computations already under way — about 100 ms together. The sequential `load` calls add up to 200 ms, so the total exceeds 300 ms. That is exactly how `async` differs from simply calling a suspend function: `suspend` on its own parallelises nothing.

title: Cancellation and finally
prompt: What still gets printed during a cancellation.
explanation: Cancellation in coroutines is cooperative: `delay` is a suspension point, it checks for cancellation and throws a `CancellationException`. The `finally` block runs, so resources can be released. But another suspend function cannot be called inside it — the coroutine is already cancelled; that needs `withContext(NonCancellable)`.

title: Non-cooperative cancellation
prompt: Cancelling a computational loop with no suspension points.
explanation: `cancel` only raises a flag: a thread cannot be stopped by force. Code with no suspension points never sees that flag and runs to the end — the “cancelled” coroutine keeps burning CPU. The cure is checking `isActive`, or calling `ensureActive()` or `yield()` inside the loop.

title: SupervisorJob and a failing child
prompt: How one coroutine's error affects its neighbour.
explanation: With an ordinary `Job` the failure of any child cancels the parent and all the other children. A `SupervisorJob` isolates the children from one another: the neighbouring coroutine lives to the end. A `CoroutineExceptionHandler` works only for a `launch` at the root of a scope — with `async` the error goes to whoever calls `await`.

title: withContext and its return value
prompt: How `withContext` differs from `launch`.
explanation: `withContext` switches the context, **waits** for the result and returns it — an ordinary sequential call that merely happens on another dispatcher. `launch` returns a `Job` and waits for nothing. Hence the rule: for a result use `withContext`, for a background task use `launch`.

title: StateFlow drops intermediate values
prompt: Will the subscriber see every value?
explanation: A `StateFlow` keeps only the latest value and conflates rapid updates: the subscriber gets the initial `0` and the current `3`, while `1` and `2` are lost. That is right for screen state and wrong for events — those call for a `SharedFlow` or a channel. A `StateFlow` also drops a repeat of the same value by `equals`.

title: collectLatest versus collect
prompt: What happens to a slow handler.
explanation: `collectLatest` cancels the previous handler as soon as a new value arrives: the processing of `1` never reaches “finished”. A plain `collect` would wait for each of them and print all four lines, holding the flow up. It is the counterpart of RxJS's `switchMap`.

title: A cold flow
prompt: How many times does the body of `flow { }` run?
explanation: A `Flow` is cold: the builder's body runs anew for every terminal operator. Two `toList` calls mean two independent runs — and therefore two network requests, if there was a request inside. `shareIn`/`stateIn` are what share a single source between subscribers.

title: Static dispatch of extensions
prompt: An extension is chosen by the declared type, not by the actual one.
explanation: Extension functions are not virtual: the compiler picks them by the **static** type of the variable, so `pet.name()` gives “an animal” even though a `Dog` is inside. Ordinary methods are resolved dynamically, and `obj.speak()` prints “child”. An extension never overrides a class's method: when the signatures match, the member wins.

title: copy and a nested reference
prompt: How deep is a `data class` copy?
code:
data class Address(var city: String)
data class User(val name: String, val address: Address)

fun main() {
    val original = User("Anna", Address("Minsk"))
    val copy = original.copy(name = "Boris")

    copy.address.city = "Vilnius"

    println(original)
    println(copy)
    println(original.address === copy.address)
}
explanation: `copy` is shallow: it copies the references to nested objects rather than the objects themselves. A change through the copy is visible in the original — exactly as with spread in JavaScript. Hence the rule: a data class's fields are best made `val` and of immutable types, or the “immutable model” turns out to be imaginary.

title: equals of a data class holding an array
prompt: Comparison through the generated `equals`.
code:
data class WithArray(val items: IntArray)
data class WithList(val items: List<Int>)

fun main() {
    println(WithArray(intArrayOf(1, 2)) == WithArray(intArrayOf(1, 2)))
    println(WithList(listOf(1, 2)) == WithList(listOf(1, 2)))
    println(intArrayOf(1, 2).contentEquals(intArrayOf(1, 2)))
}
explanation: The generated `equals` compares the fields through their own `equals`, and an array's is reference-based — two different arrays with identical contents are not equal. A `List` is compared by content. Arrays need `contentEquals`, and inside a data class hand-written `equals`/`hashCode`; the compiler even warns about it.

title: by lazy and the order of initialisation
prompt: When is a `lazy` value actually computed?
explanation: Field initialisers and `init` blocks run in declaration order when the object is created — `eager` is computed straight away even though it is declared after the `init`. `by lazy` defers the computation until first access and remembers the result: the second read computes nothing. By default `lazy` is thread-safe (`SYNCHRONIZED`).

title: What scope functions return
prompt: `let`, `run`, `apply`, `also` — the difference in the return value.
explanation: `let` and `run` return the lambda's result and differ only in how the object is reached (`it` versus `this`). `apply` and `also` return the object itself and are for configuration and side actions. Here `apply` assigned 100 and then `also` added one — so 101 is printed, and it is the very same object.

title: let on a nullable
prompt: The `?.let` idiom and what it returns.
explanation: `?.let` runs the block only for a non-null value, and `?:` supplies the fallback. An empty string is a perfectly good value, so it does get into the `let`: that is the difference from JavaScript, where `||` would have caught it too. `orEmpty()` is the short form of `?: emptyList()`.

title: when over a sealed hierarchy
prompt: Why a `when` over a sealed type needs no `else`.
code:
sealed interface Result
data class Ok(val value: Int) : Result
data class Failure(val message: String) : Result
data object Loading : Result

fun render(result: Result): String = when (result) {
    is Ok -> "ok: ${result.value}"
    is Failure -> "error: ${result.message}"
    Loading -> "loading"
}

fun main() {
    println(render(Ok(42)))
    println(render(Failure("no network")))
    println(render(Loading))
    println(Loading.toString())
}
explanation: The compiler knows every direct subclass of a sealed type, so it checks the `when` for exhaustiveness itself: add a new variant and compilation breaks wherever it was forgotten. It is the same as the `never` exhaustiveness check in TypeScript, only built in. A `data object` gives a meaningful `toString` instead of an address.

title: A non-local return from an inline function
prompt: Which function does the `return` leave?
explanation: A lambda inside an `inline` function is substituted at the call site, so a `return` in it leaves the **enclosing** function rather than the lambda: “step” is printed once and the second `action()` is never reached. That is also why a `return` works inside `forEach` — it is `inline` too. `crossinline` forbids this behaviour.

title: Platform types and !!
prompt: How `!!` differs from `?:`, and when it crashes.
explanation: `filterNotNull` removes the nulls and narrows the type to `List<String>`, `?:` supplies a replacement, and `mapNotNull` combines transformation with filtering. `!!` is the one operator that deliberately throws a `NullPointerException`: it says “I take responsibility for this not being null”, and when the author is wrong, the crash happens on exactly that line.

title: A read-only List is not immutable
prompt: What does a `List` actually guarantee?
code:
fun main() {
    val mutable = mutableListOf(1, 2, 3)
    val readOnly: List<Int> = mutable

    mutable.add(4)
    println(readOnly)

    val copy = readOnly.toList()
    mutable.add(5)
    println(copy)
    println(readOnly)
}
explanation: `List` is a read-only interface rather than an immutable collection: if a `MutableList` sits underneath, the contents change for everyone holding a reference. It is exactly the same promise as `readonly` in TypeScript. A real snapshot comes from `toList()`.

title: Sequence versus List
prompt: The order of the calls under lazy processing.
explanation: Operations on a `List` are intermediate and eager: `map` builds a whole new list, and only then does `first` search through it. A `Sequence` computes element by element and stops as soon as the result is found — on large collections that is a difference of several times over. On short lists a sequence is slower instead, because of the overhead.

title: A companion object and when it is initialised
prompt: When is the companion created?
explanation: Both a `companion object` and an `object` are initialised lazily — on first access rather than at program start. A private constructor plus a factory in the companion is the standard replacement for Java's static methods. In the bytecode the companion remains a nested class, so real statics need the `@JvmStatic` annotation.
